Getting Started: Loading the Dataset

Before you begin the practical, you need to load the required dataset into R. To ensure a smooth workflow, please follow one of the two options below:

Option 1: Using a Dedicated Folder

Create a specific folder for this assignment and place the dataset file inside it. You can then load the data using the load() function by specifying the correct file path. (Note for Windows users: Please ensure you change all backslashes \ in your copied file path to forward slashes / in R).

   For Mac users, your path will look like this:

load("/Users/your_username/Documents/folder_name/dataset_name.RData")

   For Windows users, your path will look like this:

load("C:/Users/your_username/Documents/folder_name/dataset_name.RData")

Option 2: Using an R Project

Create an R Project (.Rproj) for this assignment and store the dataset directly within that project folder. Make sure to open RStudio by double-clicking the .Rproj file. This automatically sets your working directory, allowing you to load the dataset directly without a long path:

load("dataset_name.RData")

Note for this specific lab: While the above options outline the standard workflow for local files, you do not need to download or load a .RData file for this specific lab. Today, we will access our data directly through an R package.

Lab overview

The data

We use the Auto dataset from the ISLR package, which contains characteristics of automobiles from the 1970s and early 1980s.

In this lab, we focus on two variables: - mpg: miles per gallon (fuel efficiency)
- displacement: engine displacement

The task

The goal of this lab is to predict mpg from displacement and compare models of increasing complexity/flexibility: - Linear regression - Quadratic regression - \(k\)-nearest neighbors (KNN)

Model selection is performed using the train / validation (dev) / test paradigm.

Lab structure

  1. Partition and visualize the data
  2. Train the models
  3. Evaluate and compare the models on a test set

Partition and visualize the data

  1. Load required packages

    Before you start, load the following packages:

    Hint: Use the library() function to load the required packages.

Show Answer 
library(ggplot2)
library(caret)
library(ISLR)
library(dplyr)

Note: If you already have the tidyverse package installed and loaded, you do not need to load ggplot2 and dplyr separately, as they are included in tidyverse.


  1. Partitioning the data means splitting it into training and test sets so that model performance can be evaluated fairly.

    Hint: Use set.seed(1) and the sample() function to generate indices for 80% of the rows.

Show Answer 
set.seed(1)

train_idx <- sample(nrow(Auto), size = 0.8 * nrow(Auto))

Auto_train <- Auto[train_idx, ]
Auto_test  <- Auto[-train_idx, ]


  1. Display a scatter plot with displacement on the x-axis and mpg on the y-axis. Display the cases in the training set in blue, and the cases in the test set in red.

    Hint: Use ggplot() with two geom_point() layers, specifying data = Auto_train for one and data = Auto_test for the other.

Show Answer 
ggplot() + 
  geom_point(data = Auto_train,  aes(displacement, mpg), col = "blue") +
  geom_point(data = Auto_test, aes(displacement, mpg), col = "red") +
  theme_minimal()


Training the models

Linear regression model

In this model: - Outcome variable (Y): mpg
- Predictor (X): displacement

The linear regression model to be fitted is

\[\widehat{mpg} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{displacement}\]

This model assumes a linear relationship between engine displacement and fuel efficiency. The linear regression model is fitted in R using the function lm().
If you are unfamiliar with this function, consult its help page (e.g., type ?lm in the R console) before proceeding.

  1. Fit the linear regression model to the training set and save the fitted model under the name linear.

    Hint: The function lm() has the form lm(formula, data) where formula specifies the outcome and predictor variables.

Show Answer 
linear <- lm(mpg ~ displacement, data = Auto_train)


  1. Display and interpret the summary of the fitted linear regression model.

    Hint: The function summary() provides information about the estimated coefficients, their statistical significance, and overall model fit.

Show Answer 
summary(linear)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ displacement, data = Auto_train)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -13.1999  -3.0339  -0.7054   2.2857  18.7190 
## 
## Coefficients:
##               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  35.545281   0.578811   61.41   <2e-16 ***
## displacement -0.062078   0.002663  -23.31   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 4.763 on 311 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.636,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.6348 
## F-statistic: 543.4 on 1 and 311 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


  1. Compute the training Mean Squared Error (MSE) for the linear regression model and display its value.

    The MSE measures the average squared difference between the observed values and the model predictions.

    Hint: Use the fitted model object linear and extract the residuals using the function resid().

Show Answer 
mean(resid(linear)^2)
## [1] 22.5429


Quadratic regression model

The quadratic regression model to be fitted is

\[\widehat{mpg}=\beta_0+\beta_1\cdot{displacement}+\beta_2\cdot{displacement}^2\]

The square of displacement can be included in the model formula with I(displacement^2) (the I() function literally performs the specified operation).

  1. Fit the quadratic regression model to the training data, and save the object as quadratic.

    Hint: Include I(displacement^2) in your formula inside the lm() function.

Show Answer 
quadratic <- lm(mpg ~ displacement + I(displacement^2), data = Auto_train)


  1. Display and interpret the summary of this model.

    Hint: Use the summary() function on your quadratic object.

Show Answer 
summary(quadratic)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ displacement + I(displacement^2), data = Auto_train)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -15.3759  -2.3776  -0.4853   2.1725  20.4052 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)        4.221e+01  1.307e+00  32.288  < 2e-16 ***
## displacement      -1.380e-01  1.373e-02 -10.050  < 2e-16 ***
## I(displacement^2)  1.682e-04  2.989e-05   5.627  4.1e-08 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 4.544 on 310 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.6697, Adjusted R-squared:  0.6676 
## F-statistic: 314.3 on 2 and 310 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


  1. Compute the training MSE for this model, and compare it to the training MSE of the linear model. Which model performs best on the training set? Briefly explain why this result is expected.

    Hint: Use mean(resid(quadratic)^2) and think about how adding polynomial terms affects training error.

Show Answer 
mean(resid(quadratic)^2)
## [1] 20.4538


\(k\)-nearest neighbors (KNN)

The KNN model is a nonparametric method with a key hyperparameter:
the number of nearest neighbors, \(k\).

The choice of \(k\) controls model flexibility: - small \(k\) → more flexible model
- large \(k\) → smoother model

Because of this, cross-validation is required to select an appropriate value of \(k\).

The R code for training a KNN model using 5-fold cross-validation is provided in the lecture slides.

  1. Perform a 5-fold cross validation on the training set for \(k\in\{ 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100\}\) using the function train(). Save the fitted model object under the name knn.

    Hint: In the caret package, KNN is trained with method = "knn". You can specify the values of \(k\) using tuneGrid, and control cross-validation using trainControl().

Show Answer 
knn <- train(mpg ~ displacement, 
             data = Auto_train, 
             method = "knn",
             tuneGrid = expand.grid(k = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100)),
             trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5))


  1. Display and interpret the contents of the object knn. Which value of \(k\) yields the lowest RMSE? (Remember that RMSE is the square root of the MSE). Briefly explain how cross-validation is used here to select \(k\).

    Hint: Simply type knn to view the results and look for the row with the lowest RMSE.

Show Answer 
knn
## k-Nearest Neighbors 
## 
## 313 samples
##   1 predictor
## 
## No pre-processing
## Resampling: Cross-Validated (5 fold) 
## Summary of sample sizes: 252, 250, 251, 250, 249 
## Resampling results across tuning parameters:
## 
##   k    RMSE      Rsquared   MAE     
##     1  4.807981  0.6551599  3.522589
##     2  4.691465  0.6700786  3.500333
##     5  4.415542  0.6938562  3.347389
##    10  4.366952  0.6989671  3.298348
##    25  4.305888  0.7033896  3.241467
##    50  4.375366  0.6944171  3.301234
##   100  4.666888  0.6648852  3.575024
## 
## RMSE was used to select the optimal model using the smallest value.
## The final value used for the model was k = 25.


  1. Compute the training MSE for the KNN model and compare it to the training MSEs of the linear and quadratic regression models. Which model performs best on the training set? Briefly explain why this result is expected.

    Hint: Extract the RMSE from knn$results, square it, and compare it to the previously calculated MSEs.

Show Answer 
min(knn$results$RMSE^2)
## [1] 18.54067


Visualizing the predictions

  1. To visualize and compare the fitted models, create a data frame Train that contains the training data along with the predicted values from each model. This allows us to directly compare how the linear, quadratic, and KNN models fit the training data.

    Hint: You may find the function mutate() from the dplyr package useful for adding predicted values as new columns.

Show Answer 
Train <- mutate(Auto_train, 
                pred_linear    = predict(linear),
                pred_quadratic = predict(quadratic),
                pred_knn       = predict(knn))


  1. Display a scatterplot of the training data and add the fitted curves from the three models:

  • linear regression

  • quadratic regression

  • KNN

    Use geom_line() to overlay the fitted values for each model, and give each line a different color.

    Hint: Make sure the predicted values are plotted against displacement.

Show Answer 
ggplot(Train) + 
  geom_point(aes(displacement, mpg)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = displacement, y = pred_linear), col = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(x = displacement, y = pred_quadratic), col = "red") +
  geom_line(aes(x = displacement, y = pred_knn), col = "purple") +
  theme_minimal()


Testing the models

To evaluate how well the models generalize to new data, obtain predictions for the test set and compute the MSE for each model.

The test set was not used during model training or selection, so the test MSE provides an unbiased estimate of out-of-sample performance.

  1. Create a data frame Test that contains the test data along with the predicted values from each of the fitted models.

    These predictions will be used to compute the test MSE and compare model performance on new, unseen data.

    Hint: You can use mutate() to add predicted values as new columns, and predict() to obtain predictions from each model on the Auto_test dataset.

Show Answer 
Test <- mutate(Auto_test, 
                pred_linear    = predict(linear, Auto_test),
                pred_quadratic = predict(quadratic, Auto_test),
                pred_knn       = predict(knn, Auto_test))


  1. Compute and display the MSE for the three models:

  • linear regression

  • quadratic regression

  • KNN

    Which model performs best on the test set?
    What do you conclude about the other two models — are they underfitting or overfitting the data?

    Hint: The test MSE measures how well a model generalizes to new data. Calculate the mean squared difference between mpg and each prediction column.

Show Answer 
Test %>% summarise(testMSE_linear    = mean((mpg - pred_linear)^2),
                   testMSE_quadratic = mean((mpg - pred_quadratic)^2),
                   testMSE_knn       = mean((mpg - pred_knn)^2)) 
##   testMSE_linear testMSE_quadratic testMSE_knn
## 1       16.97269          12.87248    13.27637


  1. Plot the test data and overlay the predictions from the three models:

  • linear regression

  • quadratic regression

  • KNN

    Use different colors to distinguish the fitted curves. This visualization helps assess how well each model generalizes to new data.

    Hint: Use ggplot() with Test data, mapping displacement and mpg to points, and the prediction columns to geom_line() with different colors.

Show Answer 
ggplot(Test) + 
  geom_point(aes(displacement, mpg)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = displacement, y = pred_linear), col = "blue") +
  geom_line(aes(x = displacement, y = pred_quadratic), col = "red") +
  geom_line(aes(x = displacement, y = pred_knn), col = "purple") +
  theme_minimal()


  1. (Optional) Advanced exercise: Tuning model flexibility

    This exercise is intended for students who want to explore model flexibility in more detail. Sensitivity of KNN to the choice of \(k\)

    In the KNN model, the value of \(k\) controls how flexible the model is.

    1. Using the results stored in the object knn, create a plot showing the cross-validated RMSE as a function of \(k\).
    2. Explain how the choice of \(k\) affects model bias and variance.
    3. What happens when \(k\) is very small? What happens when \(k\) is very large?

    Hint: The cross-validation results are stored in the results component of the knn object. You can pass knn$results directly into ggplot().

Show Answer 
ggplot(knn$results, aes(x = k, y = RMSE)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of neighbors (k)",
    y = "Cross-validated RMSE",
    title = "KNN performance as a function of k"
  )


END OF LAB
